knowledge_point.title: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)= (y + 1)\ln (x + 4),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y + 1)\ln (x + 4)) \\  & =\frac{y + 1}{x + 4} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y + 1)\ln (x + 4)) \\  & =\ln(x + 4)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y + 1}{x + 4} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x + 4) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y + 1}{x + 4} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x + 4) \, \mathbf j = 0 \mathbf i + 0\mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y + 1}{x + 4}=0 \\ \ln(x + 4)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y + 1=0,$ which means $y=-1.$ From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x + 4)=0,$ which means that $x=-3.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf 0$ at the point $(-3,-1).$

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)= (y + 2)\ln (x + 2),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y + 2)\ln (x + 2)) \\  & =\frac{y + 2}{x + 2} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y + 2)\ln (x + 2)) \\  & =\ln(x + 2)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y + 2}{x + 2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x + 2) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y + 2}{x + 2} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x + 2) \, \mathbf j = 0 \mathbf i + 0\mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y + 2}{x + 2}=0 \\ \ln(x + 2)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y + 2=0,$ which means $y=-2.$ From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x + 2)=0,$ which means that $x=-1.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf 0$ at the point $(-1,-2).$

knowledge_point.title: Finding the Points Where a Gradient Vanishes

question.:question/problem: Given that $f(x,y)= (y - 3)\ln (x),$ find the points $(x, y)$ where $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0.$
question.:question/worked-solution:
First, we find the partial derivatives: 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂f}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}((y - 3)\ln (x)) \\  & =\frac{y - 3}{x} \\ \frac{∂f}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}((y - 3)\ln (x)) \\  & =\ln(x)\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have

$$
\nabla f(x,y) = \dfrac {y - 3}{x} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x) \, \mathbf j.
$$

Now, we solve $\nabla f(x,y) = \mathbf 0\mathbin{:}$

$$
\dfrac {y - 3}{x} \, \mathbf i + \ln(x) \, \mathbf j = 0 \mathbf i + 0\mathbf j
$$

By equating the coefficients of $\mathbf{i}$ on both sides of the equation (and similarly with $\mathbf{j}$), we obtain

$$
\{\begin{aligned}\frac{y - 3}{x}=0 \\ \ln(x)=0.\end{aligned}
$$

From the first equation, we get $y - 3=0,$ which means $y=3.$ From the second equation, we obtain $\ln(x)=0,$ which means that $x=1.$

Therefore, $\nabla f(x,y) =\mathbf 0$ at the point $(1,3).$
